What the heck happened here?
Trashed files in Linux are available in Windows?

Linux (and other unices) hides files and directories beginning with a dot by default.

There's an option in the file manager to show these "hidden" files, often with a keyboard shortcut like alt+dot.

Trashcan may be implemented in desktop environments as a .Trash or .Trash-0 directory (or it may be in the home directory at something like ~/.local/share/Trash). "Deleting" files in a file manager or some such doesn't normally delete them but just moves them to the trash. (Windows works similarly!) Removable media such as USB drives may get their own trash on the drive--I think it depends on the desktop environment. Emptying the trash then actually removes the files.

Windows doesn't hide filenames starting with a dot, so you can see them
That's standard behaviour. In most graphic file manager pressing shift will actually delete the file(s) otherwise they are moved to trash.

Delete your files with the command line rather than a file manager. The rm command doesn't just hide the files in the bin, it deletes them. Personally, I never use a file manager on my Linux machines as it is far too slow but if you do, you need to empty the trash to actually delete the files and free up the space.
